segments.text: hi everyone in this video we will learn
how to implement automated security
scanning of Docker images with GitHub
Actions and Trivy GitHub Actions is a
continuous integration and continuous
delivery also known as CI/CD platform
that allows developers to automate their
build test and deployment pipeline if
you would like a more in-depth
explanation of GitHub Actions I linked a
YouTube tutorial I made in the
description below Trivy is a security
scanner for containers image is local
directories within a file system Git
repositories and other artifacts in this
tutorial I will show you how you can
automate container security scans with
GitHub Actions please note that the code
is available on GitHub and it is linked
Below in the description in order to
create a workflow with GitHub Actions
you need to define the workflow with a
YAML file the YAML file needs to be
saved in a special directory first you
need to create a directory called ".github"
then within that directory you need to
create another directory called
"workflows" within the newly created
directory I am going to create the YAML
file for our workflow I will name the
file trivy_scan.yml
let us get into the code first I
need to set a name for the workflow and
this will be displayed in the GitHub
actions interface next we need to Define
our trigger event a trigger event starts
a new workflow within the GitHub action
in this this case there are two trigger
events a new workflow runs whenever a
push occurs to the main branch a new
workflow will also run whenever a pull
request targeting the main branch is
created or updated in terms of DevOps it
makes sense to run a security scanner
when a push or pull request is executed
because any potential vulnerabilities
from the new code can be spotted and if
needed be addressed quickly here I am
going to define my job a job defines a
set of tasks to be executed we have a
single job here named "build" the name
gives a description of the job I'm going
to scan the latest Docker image for
Nginx using Trivy the "runs-on" key
specifies the virtual environment that
is used to generate the workflow in my
case I am using Ubuntu
20.04 which is Focal Fossa
for our job we have nine underlying
steps the first step utilizes the
actions/checkout a pre-built GitHub
action provided by GitHub this action
clones our repository into the runner
which is a temporary virtual machine
running Ubuntu Focal by setting up the
repository and the .git directory this
action enables us to make Git operations
such as committing and pushing changes
this will be essential later in the
workflow when we commit the Trivy scan
results to the repository the Second
Step retrieves the current date using a
Bash command and stores it as an
environment variable in "GITHUB_ENV" this
date will be dynamically appended to
the Trivy output files name ensuring
that each run generates a uniquely named
file by date the third step creates a
directory within the runner's file
system using Bash command this directory
will serve as the output location for
the Trivy scan results for the current
workflow run we also have to create the
directory within our original repository
the workflow creates the directory
within the runner but it does not create
it within the original directory which
is why we need to create it here the
fourth step installs Trivy on the
runner we will run the typical steps
when installing a package on a Ubuntu
machine first we will update the APT
package manager next we will install
curl and finally we will use Curl to
download and run a bash script which will
install Trivy the fifth step logs into
the GitHub container registry using a
personal access token or PAT stored in
the secret "GHCR_PAT" this step is
necessary because unauthenticated
requests to the GitHub container
registry are subject to stricter rate
limits by authenticating with a PAT the
runner has a higher rate limit and can
pull images more reliably I am going to
switch over to my browser I am going to
show you how to generate a personal
access token on GitHub and then use the
personal access token within a GitHub
repository in the top right corner I am
going to select my
profile I am going to select
settings I will scroll down and at the
bottom left I have developer settings I
will select
that on the left I am going to select
personal access tokens and I am going to
select a fine grain
token I will select generate a new token
now I can generate my token I am going
to name the token "GHCR_PAT"
by default the logged in user
is the resource owner we have our
expiration settings this is how long the
personal access token will last by
default it's set at 30 days for security
purposes it is best to set the
expiration somewhere between 30 and 90
days having a personal access token with
no expiration is a security risk there
is an option to set a description for
the personal access token I am going to
say that this is for a GitHub Action
that is going to run a Trivy scan for
the repository access I am going to
leave the default as public repositories
and I will leave defaults for the
remaining values and generate the token
we have our token here I am going to
copy the value from the clipboard as
always be careful with sharing your
token now that we have our token I am
going to go back to my repository where
I am running my workflow in my
Repository I am going to go to the
repository
settings on the left I am going to
select secrets and variables I will
select
actions I am going to create a new
repository
secret I'm going to name the secret
"GHCR_PAT" when we reference our secret
within the YAML file for the GitHub
action it will be based off of this name
and I am going to paste the value for
the PAT within the secret body I will
add the
secret I am going to go back to my code
editor to bring up the YAML file for our
workflow step six downloads the Trivy
vulnerability database when Trivy scans
a Docker image it is going to reference
this database step seven runs the Trivy
vulnerability scan in this case Trivy
scanning the latest Docker image for
Nginx for the scan I want to Output
the results into a JSON format I will
exclude any vulnerabilities that do not
have a fix available I am going to scan
for vulnerabilities in the base
operating system of the image such as
Ubuntu Focal and I am going to scan for
vulnerabilities in application
dependencies such as NPM or pip I will
have Trivy scan for vulnerabilities
designated as high medium and low
finally after the scan is complete the
results will be output into the Trivy
automation directory step eight verifies
that the results exist the bash command
prints out the content of the Trivy
automation directory to check that the
scan is there Step nine the final step
commits the changes to the original
directory an environment variable named
GitHub token is created for
authentication the token allows the
workflow to perform git operations
without requiring additional credentials
for the Git commands the identity is
configured in this case the identity for
the workflow is the GitHub action itself
the scan results are staged and
committed then the commit is pushed to
the main branch of the original
repository now that we have our YAML
file created for our workflow let us
push these changes into our GitHub
repository once we push the changes to
the GitHub repository this will initiate
the workflow we defined in our YAML file
here within my git Bash terminal first I
will run git ad period which will stage
the changes in my current working
directory next I will commit the changes
using Git commit I am going to write a
descriptive message for my commit
finally I am going to push the changes
using git push I am going to go back to
the repository to check out the workflow
on GitHub within the repository you will
know a workflow is running if you have
the name of the workflow followed by an
orange dot we can see the workflow for
the Trivy scin is currently running to
view the workflow I am going to go to
the actions tab we can see we have a few
workflows here the workflow with the
orange dot is currently running I am
going to select it we have our job
running for our workflow we can click on
it to see the underlying steps we have
our steps here if there's a check mark
then we know that the step was executed
if there is an issue with a step then a
red X will appear next to the step and a
message with the error will print out
here once a workflow has executed
successfully you will receive a green
check let us go back into our repository
and check out the output I will select
the GitHub Actions directory then the
Trivy automation directory we can see
that we have adjacent file here I will
select it and we can see here that we
were successfully able to run the scan
with Trivy on the Nginx Docker image
then save it within our repository
thanks everyone for watching I hope that
